Incubated at a constant 36 °C [T = 36 °C], the eggs of the American white pelican typically hatch after a period of 36 days [ab = 36 days]. Newly emerged chicks are altricial in their dependency on parental provisioning but are surprisingly heavy, with a recorded wet weight at birth of 110 grams [Wwb = 110 grams]. This substantial neonatal mass, coupled with the thermally controlled incubation regime, sets the stage for a rapid developmental trajectory. Field observations indicate that under the typical body temperatures of adult pelicans, which average 40.6 °C [T = 40.6 °C], young birds achieve their first sustained flight at 88 days after hatching [tx = 88 days after hatching]. This fledgling interval is notable for the intense biparental care required to support the chick through its rapid gains in both skeletal size and flight feather maturation.

Adult females of Pelecanus erythrorhynchos attain a typical ultimate wet weight of 4970 grams [Wwi = 4970 grams], a figure that positions them as one of the larger-bodied members of the Pelecanidae. Males, exhibiting the sexual size dimorphism common to the genus, reach a substantially greater maximum adult body mass of 6920 grams [Wwi = 6920 grams]. This dimorphism is thought to be linked to the species' colonial nesting strategy and the role of males in territory defense at the breeding colony. Somatic growth in this species appears to continue for an extended period before reproduction is initiated. Evidence from field studies conducted at stable thermal conditions around 40.6 °C [T = 40.6 °C] suggests that the interval between hatching and the attainment of sexual maturity is 264 days after hatching [tp = 264 days after hatching]. This relatively delayed maturation is consistent with the bird's slow life-history pace, which includes a long lifespan and deferred breeding.

The species is characterized by a remarkably long maximum lifespan, which has been documented at 54 years [am = 54 years], and such a lengthy existence, exceptional among waterbirds of comparable size, underscores a life-history strategy heavily weighted toward adult survival and repeated, low-frequency reproduction at a temperature of 40.6 °C [T = 40.6 °C]. At a typical active body temperature of 40.6 °C [T = 40.6 °C], female pelicans do not rush into their first reproductive effort. Instead, they defer their first breeding attempt until approximately 3 years after hatching [tR = approximately 3 years after hatching], a period of somatic consolidation and, presumably, social learning within large, dense colonies at a temperature of 40.6 °C [T = 40.6 °C]. The normothermic core body temperature of 40.6 °C governs the metabolic rate underpinning these slow-paced life-history events.

Reproductive output in this species is constrained by the demands of providing for large, slowly developing young. A typical clutch consists of 2 to 6 eggs per clutch [N_R_i = 2 to 6 eggs per clutch], representing a significant energetic investment for the female. Furthermore, breeding is not an annual event for all individuals; available data indicate that females generally produce only a single clutch each year [F_R_i = single clutch each year]. This reproductive frequency, which is comparatively low even among Pelecaniformes, reflects the extended period of chick rearing and the necessity of replenishing body condition between breeding seasons. The operational body temperature during these reproductive activities remains at 40.6 °C, providing a stable internal environment for the physiological processes of egg formation, incubation, and the provisioning of the altricial brood. The combination of moderate clutch size and infrequent breeding yields a low maximum annual reproductive rate of approximately 2 eggs per year [Ri = approximately 2 eggs per year] for a bird of this size.

Beyond their core life-history metrics, American white pelicans exhibit intriguing physiological adaptations to their piscivorous diet and colonial breeding habits. Their large gular pouch serves not only as a highly efficient fishing net but also as a critical organ for thermoregulation during hot weather, allowing heat dissipation through gular fluttering. The intense sociality of their breeding colonies, often on isolated islands in freshwater lakes, necessitates complex behavioral interactions during the protracted pre-breeding period extending to 264 days after hatching [tp = 264 days after hatching] at a temperature of 40.6 °C [T = 40.6 °C]. The developmental milestone of independence from provisioning, occurring at 88 days after hatching [tx = 88 days after hatching], is typically followed by a period of post-fledging parental care before full nutritional autonomy is achieved at a temperature of 40.6 °C [T = 40.6 °C]. Comparative studies with other Pelecanus species suggest that the large body mass, exemplified by the 6920 gram [Wwi = 6920 gram] adult male, is an adaptation for efficient long-distance soaring flight and for subduing relatively large fish prey in cooperative foraging bouts.
